entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Read about Canadian history from 1800-1900 through biographies, primary source documents, history spines, and historical fiction. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries.

This topic is included in the following course(s): History: Grades 11-12 (Canada)

links.label: Not One Way to Mark a Book

blocks.text:
• Take a second to recall what you read previously in the same book or topic.

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Read the selection assigned OR read for the number of minutes allocated, leaving time for narration and mapwork. Use whichever guide (i.e., pages or minutes) works best for you. You want to read enough to be interesting, but not so much that you feel overwhelmed.

• If a book is challenging for you as a student, try stopping to narrate to yourself silently for a minute every now and then to make sure you are tracking. You might also want to read aloud to yourself. Or you might want to listen to an audiobook version of the text and read along with it. 

• If a book is an easy read, enjoy the ride! 

• Keep an eye out for quotes to put in your commonplace book or events or characters to put down in your Book of Centuries.

• Process and integrate your reading by narrating either orally or in writing. Some lesson plans will give you a suggestion of how best to narrate. 

• To keep yourself on track, you might want to set a timer, so you stop reading with enough time to narrate.

• After your narration, think about how what you read connects to other subjects, other books, and other things you've read, watched, or seen in the past or present. 

• Share any ideas that are particularly interesting to you with your fellow classmates, teachers, parents, friends, or others. You might even want to do a bit more reading or research on something on your own time in the afternoon or evenings.

These lessons are written directly to the student, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. Accountability components are added to facilitate teacher/student discussion and growing independence. 

Those educating at home might pick one or two history lessons to read aloud with their students to keep up the habit of oral narration and foster conversation and relationship, and then simply give students these lesson plans and the rest of the books and check in with them throughout the term for conversation, support, and accountability. 

It is valuable for those in a classroom setting to also have a mix of lessons that students complete themselves silently and others read aloud and narrated together. Classroom settings lend themselves well to additional discussion and sharing at the end of lessons, after everyone has narrated either together or independently in writing.

lessons.title: 40m Canadian History: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Introduction, David Thompson
⍞ Materials: A History of Canada in Ten Maps

✂ GATHER SUPPLIES: You will need a notebook for Canadian history where you will be writing and drawing. We recommend dot grid and blank notebooks, but any kind will do.

PREP: Print a copy of the blank map of Canada without borders. You can use this together with your notebook to mark places and chart routes throughout this course.
∞ Map Link: Printable Map of Canada without Borders

➜ INTRO
In this course, we will learn about the history of Canada between 1800-1900. The five books are intended to work together to give a chronological overview of this historical period. Two of the books - The History of Canada in Ten Maps and The Making of Canada - we are starting partway through, since the first halves were read during Rotation 2. If you did not read them during Rotation 2, you may wish to read the first halves on your own time; however, you can also start partway through without missing content for this course.
At the beginning of this century, Canada was a collection of separate British colonies and was vulnerable to invasion by the newly independent nation of the United States to the south. Yet by the end of the century, Canada was a self-governing country of seven provinces and two territories, with a transcontinental railway that stretched from coast to coast. This class will explore many of the changes that took place during this time.

➜ DISCUSS
What do you remember about Canadian History before 1800? What do you already know about the period between 1800-1900? Jot down a few notes for yourself of any people, places, or events that you think might be relevant. Also, write down any questions you might have about this period of Canadian history.

➜ READ
1\. The Canadian Encyclopedia
As you work through the course, you should find time to fill out a History Chart for the years 1800-1900, or continue to update your Book of Centuries if you have one. The Canadian Encyclopedia is an excellent source for research and information to add to your notebooking.
∞ Article Link: David Thompson Biography

2\. The History of Canada in Ten Maps
p.227-236 "In the dead of winter" - "until the twentieth century."

➜ NARRATE
Narrate in a way that helps you interact with the ideas in the reading. For some, that might be narrating orally or silently to yourself, in writing, by drawing a map, a diagram or a picture, writing a diary/letter from the point of view of one of the characters, describing what happened, or writing a bulleted list of points and questions. For others, it might be helpful to make marks in the book as you read and then narrate as you look at what you marked in the chapter. Experiment and see what works well for you, and you can vary your approach week to week. Also, strive to make connections to ideas, events, and people you have come across in previous readings you have done.

➜ DISCUSS
Most lessons will include optional questions for further discussion, written response, or reflection.
• What made David Thompson such a successful cartographer and explorer? How much was his own skill, and how much was it his willingness to heed and learn from indigenous assistance, knowledge, and practices?
• Why was David Thompson's work so important for fur trading companies and the government?
lessons.teacherNotes:

Episode 5: A Question of Loyalties (1775-1815)
Episode 6: The Pathfinders (1670-1850)
Episode 7: Rebellion and Reform (1815-1850)
Episode 8: The Great Enterprise (1850-1867)
Episode 9: From Sea to Sea (1867-1873)
Episode 10: Taking the West (1873-1896)

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
David Thompson, cont.
⍞ Materials: A History of Canada in Ten Maps

➜ ANNOTATE
As your ability to read higher-level books in high school grows, it is helpful to learn new ways to interact with the text while you are reading to help you grasp what the author is saying. Non-fiction books are usually good candidates for annotating while you read. Maybe you want to underline the main ideas or interesting points. Maybe you want to put a question mark in the margin if something is unclear. Think about how to help yourself engage with the information in the book to make it your own. Experiment with different ways to do that. Some students do best by recording themselves talking about the reading, while others may need to discuss the material with another person. Whatever you do, your annotations should help you to further solidify the main points or ideas in your mind. Write down any questions, comments, or connections that arise from your review of your annotations after reading. Try different ways and discuss your observations about what works well and what doesn't with your teacher.
Explore ways that might be most helpful for you as you read each week. Advances in technology make many more annotation options available to serve us and our various ways of processing. Some might do great with a pencil and a book, while others might benefit from colors, Post-its, or speech-to-text options.
Linked are two documents to give you some more ideas for what it means to annotate a text. Charlotte Mason talked about ways to use books in School Education on p.180-181 if you are interested in reading her words on the topic, too.
Today's reading and the next are shorter to allow you time to read the documents and practice annotating. For today, if you are new to this, start simply by putting a mark in the margin or a Post-it flag when you come across a main idea or an important point the author is making. For others who have been doing this already, see what new ways you might want to experiment with this term.

∞ Article Link: How to Mark a Book
∞ PDF Link: Not One Way to Mark a Book
∞ Book Link: School Education p.180

lessons.title: 40m Canadian History: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 3
lessons.body:
The War of 1812: Charles de Salaberry
⍞ Materials: The Making of Canada

➜ INTRO
The Making of Canada is a collection of biographical vignettes that will introduce you to largely forgotten historical figures who were nevertheless vital to significant events in Canada's history. You will read this book alongside A History of Canada in Ten Maps to build a chronological view of this historical period.

➜ READ & ANNOTATE
p.148-158 "Almost thirty years after" - "what they achieved at Châteauguay."

➜ NARRATE
Choose the best way for you to narrate what you read.

➜ DISCUSS
• The War of 1812 is usually synonymous with the battles near Upper Canada that occurred in 1812, especially the Battle of Queenston Heights, where Sir Isaac Brock was killed. Why was Lower Canada a more strategically critical region to protect, according to Koabel? And why might French Canadians have been hesitant at first to help defend it? What changed?
• Why was the Battle at Châteauguay a distinctly Canadian episode of the War of 1812? What are some of the possible reasons why it is not commemorated by English-speaking or French-speaking Canadians today?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
To learn more about the War of 1812 (which lasted until 1815), visit this virtual exhibit at the Canadian War Museum to learn about the war from four different perspectives.
∞ Link: 1812 Virtual Exhibition

The Red River Colony and the Pemmican Wars: Cuthbert Grant, cont.
⍞ Materials: The Making of Canada

➜ DISCUSS
• The violent confrontation on June 19, 1816, has been called the "Seven Oaks Massacre," the "Battle of Seven Oaks," and the "Victory at the Frog Plain." How does the naming of an event shape our interpretation of it?
• Why do you think the author chose to focus on Cuthbert Grant in telling this story from Canadian History?
• How did the competition between the rival fur trading companies lead to tensions in the Red River colony? And how did these tensions shape Métis identity?

Mapping the Arctic Frontier
⍞ Materials: The History of Canada in Ten Maps

➜ RECAP

➜ INTRO
What do you know already about the quest to find the Northwest Passage? Which other explorers had attempted it? Why was it a desirable route to discover?

➜ READ & ANNOTATE
p.273-285 "Dr. John Richardson" - "an almost Herculean effort."

➜ NARRATE
Choose the best way for you to narrate what you read.

➜ VIEW
Locate York Factory and Fort Chipewyan
∞ Map Link: Fur trade routes of the Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company, circa 1820

➜ DISCUSS
• Why do you think Great Britain made arctic exploration a priority after the conclusion of the Napoleonic Wars?
• How would you characterize John Franklin's leadership style? What were his strengths and weaknesses?
• Imagine you were making an overland journey from Hudson Bay to the Arctic. What would you need to bring? How would you balance bringing all the necessities with the limitation of space and the strength needed to carry your own gear?

Newfoundland: James Landrigan and Patrick Morris
⍞ Materials: The Making of Canada

➜ NARRATE
Choose the best way for you to narrate what you read.

➜ DISCUSS
• What was the "truck system," and how did it contribute to both the establishment of permanent settlements and economic instability in nineteenth-century Newfoundland?
• How did religion impact the Newfoundland reformers and their detractors?
• Does Patrick Morris's campaign for the establishment of a colonial government in Newfoundland remind you of other events you've learned about in Canadian history?

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 12

⍞ Materials: The Making of Canada

➜ RECAP

➜ NARRATE
Choose the best way for you to narrate what you read.

➜ DISCUSS
• What were some of the grievances that led to the Upper Canada Rebellion of 1837-1838?
• How would you describe Ogle Gowan's legacy? What impact did he have on Canadian politics in the 1830s?
• What did you learn from today's reading about the history of Canada's relationship with the United States?

lessons.title: 40m Canadian History: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 13
lessons.body:
Summer Rambles: Anna Brownell Jameson
⍞ Materials: Early Voices

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about the Upper Canada Rebellions of 1837-1838 from the last reading?

➜ INTRO
In your reading from the last lesson, you learned that Ogle Gowan stood for election in 1834 with Attorney General Robert Jameson. Today, we will read an account written by Jameson's wife Anna, who joined him in Canada for several years before returning to England. This is the first of a number of selections we will read this year from Early Voices: Portraits of Canada by Women Writers, 1639-1914. This book is used over several years in high school, and, since the selections are assigned chronologically, the book is read out of order.
• If you could travel back in time to Canada 200 years ago, what do you think would be some of the most significant differences you would find in the natural world?

➜ READ & ANNOTATE
p.113-125 "Anna Brownell Jameson" - "my rock on Lake Huron."

➜ NARRATE
Choose the best way for you to narrate what you read.

➜ DISCUSS
• What kind of observer is Jameson? What draws her attention? What does she notice about other people? What interests her?
• What might historians find useful in a document like this one? How reliable is she as a historical source?
• What did you learn about life in nineteenth-century Canada?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
Remember when reading primary source documents such as this one that some of the language, attitudes, assumptions, and observations will come across as derogatory to modern readers, yet should be interpreted within their historical context. 

• EXTRA HELPING
Learn more about Anna Brownell Jameson's life.
 ∞ Link: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Anna Brownell Jameson

➜ DISCUSS

• What did you learn about life in nineteenth-century Canada, particularly life for an unmarried woman?

The Metis Nation: James Sinclair
⍞ Materials: The Making of Canada

➜ DISCUSS
• How was James Sinclair a different leader from Cuthbert Grant? What had changed for the Métis people in the thirty-three years since the Battle of Seven Oaks?
• What challenges did the Red River settlement present to the Hudson Bay Company? How did HBC address them, and what was the outcome?
• Koabel writes that "Many historians date the birth of the Metis Nation not from the Battle of the Seven Oaks, in 1816, but from Sayer's trial in 1849." Why do you think that is?

lessons.title: 40m Canadian History: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 25
lessons.body:
James Douglas
⍞ Materials: The Making of Canada

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about Mary Ann Shadd's Plea for Emigration from the last reading?
Take a moment to review your annotations. How is your annotation system working for you? Consider trying something different today.

➜ READ & ANNOTATE
p.262-278 "In the eighteenth century" - "British Columbia remained British."

➜ NARRATE
Choose the best way for you to narrate what you read.

➜ DISCUSS
• Explain why the discovery of gold in the Fraser Valley instigated such a diplomatic crisis for James Douglas. How would you describe him as a leader? What strategies did he use to ensure British Columbia remained British?
• Based on the situation in British Columbia, can you identify some larger issues that might have spurred politicians to push for Confederation over the following decade? How would you describe the relationship between British North America and the United States as it unfolded in this one location?
• Koabel states that "the instability and disorder of 1858 pushed Douglas and Begbie to weave the infrastructure of a proper colony out of whole cloth. In this, they were largely successful" (278). What do you think he means by this? Consider that to "weave something out of whole cloth" means a fabrication or a creation of something with little basis in reality.

terms.content:
· (The History of Canada in Ten Maps) Adam Shoalts writes that "Explorers might make the first maps, but the final ones are usually made by armies." How is this statement true for the War of 1812? Are there other events from history where this perspective holds true? 
OR Explain why the British navy turned its attention to the Arctic after the end of the Napoleonic Wars. What were its aims there? What role did the unknown regions of the Arctic play in the nineteenth-century view of the world?

· (The Making of Canada): Describe the role either Cuthbert Grant or James Sinclair played in the identity of the Métis Nation.
OR Define the two sides of the debate between Mary Ann Shadd and the Bibbs over the Refugee Home Society, and between Shadd and Frederick Douglass over the issue of emigration.

· (The Making of Canada) Koabel highlights several instances where Canada has been the site of an intended or actual invasion or conflict meant to incite a larger battle (such as an Anglo-American war), or a change elsewhere in the world (such as the Fenian goal for an Irish uprising). Describe and compare two or more examples of these conflicts and consider what role they played, if any, in encouraging British North American colonies to join in Confederation.
OR
(The Unweaving) Describe the Red River Settlement, its variety of inhabitants, and the Métis way of life based on what you have read in the novel so far.

· (How Different It Was) Compare life today in your region of Canada to what life was like in that region in the nineteenth century.
OR
Imagine you have just arrived at a piece of uncleared prairie land that you have acquired and hope to farm. What are your priorities? What do you need to provide for yourself and your family immediately? How will you accomplish these tasks?

· (How Different It Was and Early Voices) Choose one reading from Early Voices and compare it to the historical survey of nineteenth-century Canadian society from How Different It Was. In what ways does the individual's account illustrate the elements of Canadian society that Goodspeed describes? Are there ways that it complicates or challenges Goodspeed's bird's-eye view of society as a whole?
OR
Choose two or more readings from Early Voices and compare the women's experiences of life in nineteenth-century Canada. What were their circumstances? What challenges did they face? What would they talk about if they could meet each other in person? You can write this as a creative dialogue if you prefer.

· (The Unweaving) Why did Cheryl Parisien choose The Unweaving as the title of the book? Consider all the mentions of weaving, sewing, other fabric arts, and the symbolism of the Métis sash (called the "saencheur flayshii," or arrow belt). Include references to specific events in the novel.
OR
Describe all you remember about the circumstances that led to the Red River Resistance of 1869, and its outcome, based on the events of the novel. You can write this as a historical report or from the perspective of one of the characters in the novel. You can be creative and write it as a letter, an interview, or another form of your choosing.
